scope: Intermittent HTTP 500 investigation on the isolated catevia-free-feasibility Worker plus live fault-injection attempts against the real application password adapter. No Catevia credential, user, database, or production route was used.
question: The 2026-09-24 record listed an unexplained intermittent HTTP 500 under concurrent bcrypt load. Is there a single root cause, and does the bounded retry convert it into a success?

attempt1.change: redeploy with identical Durable Object class code
attempt1.conclusion: A redeploy that does not change the object class code performs no Durable Object reset, so this attempt did not exercise the hypothesis.

attempt2.change: added PASSWORD_CPU_VERSION and a computeVersion method to the PasswordCpu class so the deployed object code genuinely differs, plus a structured PASSWORD_CPU_RETRY log
attempt2.clientSideFailureMode: TypeError fetch failed after about 42 s with no HTTP status
attempt2.conclusion: Even with a real object-code change, no code-update reset was observed while requests were in flight. The reset is a rare, non-deterministic event rather than a routine consequence of deploying.

rootCausesIdentified.status: proven once, by Cloudflare Observability on 2026-09-24
rootCausesIdentified.evidence: Durable Object AuthCpuProbe event at 13:30:12.410 GMT+7 with the exact message 'Durable Object reset because its code was updated.', trace 0fb8c979c2c84d02cabe71f65b64c71d also containing the parent /probe/bcrypt-sharded HTTP error
rootCausesIdentified.classification: deploy lifecycle, not a defect in Catevia code
rootCausesIdentified.mitigation: server/src/utils/passwordCompute.ts retries exactly one retryable RPC error, matches that exact message, never retries .overloaded, and never retries a database write, session, lockout, or audit event
rootCausesIdentified.residual: the retry branch has unit evidence and is now observable in tail, but no live proof exists because the reset cannot be forced on demand

rootCausesIdentified.evidence: A real unknown-account login on staging returned HTTP 500 traced by wrangler tail to LibsqlError SERVER_ERROR HTTP status 522 in the DB-backed rate limiter, with 19,469 ms wall time and 21 ms Worker CPU; a direct Node query to the same database also failed once with a TypeError after 10,666 ms
rootCausesIdentified.classification: upstream database path, not Workers CPU and not bcrypt
rootCausesIdentified.mitigation: placement.region aws:us-east-1 on the Worker; after placement, health 336-962 ms and unknown-account login 401 in 1,827-4,375 ms, 4 of 4 cycles clean
rootCausesIdentified.residual: eight requests in one sample do not establish a failure rate

rootCausesIdentified.evidence: 8 of 20 requests failed client-side with TypeError fetch failed after about 42 s and no HTTP status, in the same window where 12 requests returned 200 and the Worker tail recorded zero errors or exceptions
rootCausesIdentified.classification: client to edge network path; not a Worker HTTP 500 at all
rootCausesIdentified.mitigation: no server change; these requests never reached application code, so they must not be counted as backend errors
rootCausesIdentified.residual: the 2026-09-24 no-status TypeError is now explained as the same class of failure

rootCausesIdentified.evidence: Two HTTP 500s at 2026-09-24T03:39:59.974Z and 2026-09-24T04:56:27.261Z have only parent HTTP errors and the probe's old generic catch log; the raw tail was not retained
rootCausesIdentified.mitigation: none available; the probe now keeps a structured error record instead of a generic catch log
rootCausesIdentified.residual: cannot be attributed without retained evidence; deployment history shows updates before both, but timing alone does not prove a reset

conclusions: There is no single bcrypt CPU root cause. The measured front-Worker CPU for this work is 0-1 ms against a 10 ms cap, and the Durable Object used 354-669 ms p50 CPU with zero exceeded-CPU events.
The 500s seen during bcrypt load were caused by a deploy lifecycle reset and by Turso upstream connectivity, not by password hashing running out of CPU.
A further class of failure that was recorded as a possible server error is actually a client-side network failure with no HTTP response.
Two early 500s remain unattributable and are reported as unknown rather than assigned to a cause.
codeChangesMadeForDiagnosability: server/src/cloudflare/passwordCpu.js: PASSWORD_CPU_VERSION marker and computeVersion so a probe can prove which object code served a request
server/src/utils/passwordCompute.ts: structured PASSWORD_CPU_RETRY log with reason, error class, and attempt, containing no secret material
server/src/__tests__/passwordCompute.test.ts: retry log assertions plus a retryable-RPC retry case, 6 of 6 passing
